entry:
Differential survival and reproduction of individuals owing to differences in their observable characteristics, a key mechanism of [[Evolution|evolution]] that changes the heritable traits of a [[Population (biology)|population]] over generations. Variation of traits, both genotypic and phenotypic, exists within all populations, and traits that facilitate survival and reproductive success are more likely to be passed on. Selection acts on existing variation, which arises mainly from mutation and recombination, and does not direct the production of adaptive variations. Some traits spread because they suit their environments; others because mating partners prefer them, a process called sexual selection.

[[Charles Darwin]] popularised the term, contrasting it with artificial selection, in which human breeders intentionally favour desirable traits. For Darwin it resulted from three kinds of process: inheritance, variation, and the struggle for existence, which included both competition and cooperation. Classical thinkers such as Empedocles and the Roman poet [[Lucretius]] had suggested that nature randomly produces many creatures and that only those able to provide for themselves and reproduce persist; [[Aristotle]] criticised the idea. [[Alfred Russel Wallace]] independently formulated the theory, and the two men's papers were presented jointly in 1858. Darwin elaborated it in his 1859 book *[[On the Origin of Species]]*, written before a valid theory of heredity existed.

The union of Darwinian evolution with classical genetics formed the modern synthesis of the mid-20th century. Twenty-first-century biologists have challenged its gene-centred view, producing several extended evolutionary syntheses, while molecular genetics has given rise to evolutionary developmental biology. Genotypes can also change slowly by random [[Genetic drift|genetic drift]], but natural selection remains the primary explanation for adaptive evolution. Its effects include beak shape in Darwin's finches and pesticide resistance in insects.

Physical world or universe in the broadest sense, comprising the laws, elements, and phenomena of the material world, life included. Humans are part of nature, although human activity, or humanity as a whole, is often described as at odds with it or even separate from and superior to it.

In narrower uses the word refers to geology and wildlife, to the realm of living beings, or to the processes of inanimate things, such as weather and the geology of the Earth. It often means the [[Natural environment]] or wilderness: wild animals, rocks, forests, and generally whatever has not been substantially altered by human intervention. This sense implies a distinction between the natural and the artificial, the latter being brought into being by a human [[Mind|mind]]. Depending on context, "natural" may also be contrasted with the unnatural or the [[Supernatural|supernatural]]. Manufactured objects are not usually counted as part of nature unless qualified, as in "human nature".

The English word comes from Old French *nature*, derived from [[Latin]] *natura*, "essential qualities, innate disposition", which literally meant "birth". In ancient philosophy *natura* mostly translated the Greek *physis*, which originally referred to the intrinsic characteristics of plants, animals, and other things as they develop of their own accord. Pre-Socratic philosophers, especially [[Heraclitus]], gave the term a dynamic sense and extended it to the physical universe as a whole.

With the rise of the modern scientific method, nature came to be seen as a passive reality organized and moved by divine laws. After the [[Industrial Revolution]] it increasingly meant the part of reality not subject to intentional human intervention. Some traditions, such as that of Rousseau and American [[Transcendentalism]], considered it sacred, while Hegel and Marx treated it as a mere backdrop to divine providence or human history. A vitalist vision of nature, closer to the pre-Socratic one, was reborn at the same time, especially after [[Charles Darwin]].

Field of study and practice concerned with determining position and with monitoring and controlling the movement of a craft or vehicle from one place to another. It has four general categories: land, marine, aeronautic, and space navigation. All techniques involve locating the navigator's position relative to known locations or patterns, and in a broader sense the term covers any skill involving the determination of position and direction, including orienteering and pedestrian navigation.

Polynesian navigation is probably the earliest form of open-ocean navigation, relying on memory and on observation of the stars, weather, wildlife, and wave size. Among the first proper instruments was the [[Compass|compass]], of Chinese origin from the Han dynasty; the Song dynasty adopted it for sea navigation in the 11th century, and its first recorded use in Western Europe and the Islamic world dates from around 1190. The oldest record of a sea [[Astrolabe|astrolabe]] is from 1295, and Portuguese navigators are credited with perfecting it. Among the oldest surviving marine charts is the Carta Pisana, dated to 1275. The backstaff, invented by John Davis in 1595, overcame the errors of the cross-staff.

Widespread open-sea navigation began in the [[Age of Discovery]] of the 15th century. The Portuguese explored the Atlantic coast of Africa from 1418, and Bartolomeu Dias reached the Indian Ocean in 1488. In 1492 the Spanish monarchs funded [[Christopher Columbus]]'s westward expedition across the Atlantic, and in 1498 [[Vasco da Gama]] reached India by sailing around Africa. The first circumnavigation of the earth was completed in 1522 by the expedition led by [[Ferdinand Magellan]] and finished by Juan Sebastián Elcano.

Later advances in mathematics, including logarithms and spherical trigonometry, allowed more accurate navigation from the 1700s. The problem of [[Longitude|longitude]] was solved in the 18th century by John Harrison's marine chronometer (1735) and the sextant (1757). The 20th century brought radio ranges (1926), LORAN (1944), and inertial navigation (1950). The [[Global Positioning System]] reached full operational capability in 1995, and other satellite systems include Galileo, GLONASS, and BeiDou.

South African anti-apartheid revolutionary, politician, and philanthropist, president of South Africa (1994–99), the country's first black head of state and the first elected in a fully representative democratic election.

Born in Mvezo into the Thembu royal family, he studied law at the University of Fort Hare and the University of the Witwatersrand and worked as a lawyer in [[Johannesburg]]. He joined the [[African National Congress]] (ANC) in 1943 and co-founded its Youth League in 1944. After the National Party government established [[Apartheid|apartheid]], a system of racial segregation, he and the ANC committed themselves to its overthrow. He rose to prominence through the 1952 Defiance Campaign and the 1955 Congress of the People and was unsuccessfully prosecuted in the 1956 Treason Trial. Though initially committed to non-violent protest, in 1961 he co-founded the militant Umkhonto we Sizwe and led a sabotage campaign. Arrested in 1962, he was sentenced to [[Life imprisonment|life imprisonment]] in the Rivonia Trial.

Mandela served 27 years in prison, mainly on Robben Island. President F. W. de Klerk released him in 1990, and the two negotiated an end to apartheid and organised the 1994 multiracial election, which the ANC won. They shared the 1993 Nobel Peace Prize. Mandela led a broad coalition government that promulgated a new constitution, created the Truth and Reconciliation Commission to investigate past human rights abuses, and pursued land reform, poverty reduction, and expanded healthcare. He mediated in the Pan Am Flight 103 bombing trial and was Secretary-General of the [[Non-Aligned Movement]] from 1998 to 1999. He declined a second term and was succeeded by his deputy, Thabo Mbeki, then worked against poverty and [[HIV/AIDS]] through the Nelson Mandela Foundation.

Mandela was controversial for much of his life. Critics on the right denounced him as a communist terrorist; some on the radical left thought him too eager to reconcile with apartheid's supporters; others have criticised civilian casualties from Umkhonto we Sizwe bombings and his ties to [[Fidel Castro]] and [[Muammar Gaddafi]]. He received more than 250 honours and is often called Madiba, or Father of the Nation, in South Africa.

Wide-scale transition of many human cultures in Afro-Eurasia from a lifestyle of hunting and gathering to one of agriculture and settlement, also called the First Agricultural Revolution. The term was coined by V. Gordon Childe in *Man Makes Himself* (1936), who used "revolution" to denote the degree of change.

The domestication of various plants and animals occurred independently in separate parts of the world, beginning in the Holocene epoch about 11,700 years ago, after the last Ice Age. The process has been dated to 10,000–8,000 BCE in the [[Fertile Crescent]], where cereals such as barley and animals such as sheep and goats were domesticated, and perhaps 8000 BCE at the Kuk Early Agricultural Site in [[Papua New Guinea]]. Everywhere it is associated with a shift from nomadic [[Hunter-gatherer|hunter-gatherer]] life to settled, farming communities.

Surplus, plannable food supplies allowed larger populations in permanent, densely populated villages and towns. Irrigation and deforestation transformed the natural environment, and widespread accompanying developments included pottery, polished stone tools, and rectangular houses. In many regions agriculture caused episodes of rapid population growth, called the Neolithic demographic transition. Seasonal planning encouraged division of labour and specialization, and trading networks brought farmers into contact with outside groups. These developments provided the basis for centralized administrations, hierarchical ideologies, writing, non-portable art and architecture, and greater property ownership. The earliest known civilization arose in [[Sumer]] in southern Mesopotamia (c. 6,500 BP), heralding the [[Bronze Age]].

Agriculture also had costs. It greatly narrowed the diversity of foods available and reduced nutritional quality compared with hunting and foraging. Reliance on a few staple crops can harm health: [[Maize|maize]], for example, is deficient in the amino acids lysine and tryptophan and is a poor source of iron. Denser settlements and livestock increased parasites and disease, and grain storage attracted insects and rodents. The sequence in which Neolithic characteristics emerged remains debated and is understood to vary from place to place rather than follow universal laws of social evolution.

Eighth and farthest known planet from the [[Sun]], an ice giant named after the Roman god of the sea. It is the fourth-largest planet in the Solar System by diameter, the third most massive, and the densest giant planet, with 17 times the mass of Earth. It has no well-defined solid surface and orbits the Sun once every 164.8 years at a distance of 30.1 astronomical units (4.5 billion km).

Neptune is the only planet not first found by direct observation. Unexpected deviations in the orbit of [[Uranus]] led Alexis Bouvard to hypothesize an unknown perturbing body, and after his death John Couch Adams and Urbain Le Verrier independently predicted its position mathematically. Johann Gottfried Galle observed it with a telescope on September 23, 1846, within a degree of Le Verrier's prediction. Galileo's drawings of 1612–13 had already recorded its position, but he mistook it for a fixed star. Its largest moon, [[Triton (moon)|Triton]], was discovered shortly afterward; the other moons were not located telescopically until the 20th century.

Because of its distance, Neptune is hard to study from Earth; detailed observations awaited the [[Hubble Space Telescope]] and large ground-based telescopes with adaptive optics. [[Voyager 2]], which flew past on August 25, 1989, remains the only spacecraft to visit. The atmosphere is mainly hydrogen and helium with traces of hydrocarbons and possibly nitrogen, and a higher proportion of ices such as water, ammonia, and methane than in Jupiter and Saturn. Traces of [[Methane|methane]] and [[Rayleigh scattering]] make the planet appear faintly blue. The interior is primarily ices and rock.

Unlike Uranus, Neptune has active, consistently visible weather. Voyager 2 found a Great Dark Spot comparable to Jupiter's [[Great Red Spot]]; a newer main dark spot and a smaller one were identified in 2018. Winds, the strongest sustained of any planet, reach 2,100 km/h. Cloud-top temperatures approach 55 K (−218 °C), while the planet's centre is about 5,400 K (5,100 °C). A faint, fragmented ring system was discovered in 1984 and confirmed by Voyager 2.

Highly complex part of an animal that coordinates its actions and sensory information by transmitting signals to and from different parts of its body. It detects environmental changes affecting the body and works with the [[Endocrine system|endocrine system]] to respond to them. Nervous tissue first arose in wormlike organisms about 550 to 600 million years ago.

In vertebrates the system has two main parts: the [[Central nervous system]] (CNS), consisting of the brain and spinal cord, and the [[Peripheral nervous system]] (PNS), consisting mainly of nerves, enclosed bundles of long fibers called axons that connect the CNS to the rest of the body. Motor (efferent) nerves carry signals from the brain, and sensory (afferent) nerves carry information to the CNS. The PNS divides into the somatic and autonomic systems; the autonomic system has sympathetic, parasympathetic, and enteric branches, which respectively mobilize energy in emergencies, act during relaxation, and control the gastrointestinal system.

Nervous tissue is defined by the [[Neuron|neuron]], a cell that sends electrochemical impulses rapidly and precisely along axons. Signals pass to other cells through electrical synapses or by release of [[Neurotransmitter|neurotransmitters]] at chemical synapses, and a receiving cell may be excited, inhibited, or otherwise modulated. Connections among neurons form circuits and networks that generate an organism's perception of the world and determine its behavior. Glial cells provide structural and metabolic support.

Nervous systems occur in most multicellular animals but vary greatly in complexity. Only [[Sponge|sponges]], placozoans, and mesozoans lack one. Comb jellies and cnidarians, which include anemones, hydras, corals, and jellyfish, have a diffuse nerve net. Other animals, apart from a few worms, have a brain, a central cord or two parallel cords, and nerves radiating from them. Size ranges from a few hundred cells in the simplest worms to around 300 billion cells in African elephants.

Malfunction can result from genetic defects, trauma, toxicity, infection, or senescence. The medical specialty of [[Neurology|neurology]] treats its disorders, and [[Neuroscience|neuroscience]] is the field that studies the system.

Subatomic particle, symbol n or n⁰, with no electric charge and a mass slightly greater than that of a [[Proton|proton]]. Neutrons are found, together with a similar number of protons, in the [[Atomic nucleus|nuclei]] of atoms, and atoms of an element that differ only in neutron number are called [[Isotope|isotopes]]. A neutron is not an elementary particle but a baryon composed of three [[Quark|quarks]], one up and two down. A free neutron decays spontaneously into a proton, an electron, and an antineutrino, with a mean lifetime of about 15 minutes.

In 1920 [[Ernest Rutherford]] suggested that the nucleus contained neutral particles, then imagined as a proton and electron bound together, and in 1921 W. D. Harkins named the hypothetical particle a neutron. The proton–electron model became inconsistent with quantum theory and with observed nuclear spins. In 1931 Walther Bothe and Herbert Becker found that alpha particles from polonium striking beryllium, boron, or lithium produced an unusually penetrating radiation, which they took to be gamma rays. Irène and Frédéric Joliot-Curie showed that it ejected high-energy protons from paraffin. [[James Chadwick]] then demonstrated that the radiation consisted of uncharged particles with about the proton's mass. The discovery, made in 1932, won him the 1935 Nobel Prize in Physics. Werner Heisenberg and others quickly developed a proton–neutron model of the nucleus, which explained nuclear spins, and in 1934 Enrico Fermi explained beta decay.

The discovery led to rapid developments: Fermi bombarded heavier elements with neutrons, and [[Nuclear fission]] was discovered in 1938. The first self-sustaining nuclear reactor, Chicago Pile-1, followed in 1942 and the first nuclear weapon, the Trinity test, in 1945. Neutrons are essential to nuclear power, and they contribute to the nucleosynthesis of elements in stars. [[Neutron star]]s consist of neutrons at nuclear density. Free neutrons do not directly ionize atoms but indirectly cause ionizing radiation, so they can be a biological hazard. Research reactors, neutron generators, and spallation sources supply them for irradiation and neutron scattering experiments.

City (pop., 2026 est.: 8,586,038), largest in the United States, at the southern tip of New York State on New York Harbor. It comprises five boroughs, Manhattan, Brooklyn, Queens, the Bronx, and Staten Island, each coextensive with its county. Covering 778.2 sq km, it is the most densely populated major city in the country and has more than double the population of Los Angeles. The metropolitan area has more than 20.1 million residents and the combined statistical area about 22.5 million, both the largest in the U.S. An estimated 800 languages are spoken in the city, and its metropolitan region has the world's largest foreign-born population, about 5.9 million as of 2023.

The area was home to Algonquians, including Munsee-speaking Lenape. Giovanni da Verrazzano made the first documented European visit to the harbor in 1524, and Henry Hudson rediscovered it in 1609 while searching for the Northwest Passage for the [[Dutch East India Company]]. Dutch colonists established Fort Amsterdam on [[Manhattan]] around 1624; the settlement was named New Amsterdam in 1626 and chartered as a city in 1653. England took control in 1664 and renamed it for the Duke of York, later [[James II of England|James II]]; the name was made permanent in 1674. New York was the national capital from 1785 until 1790, and the modern city was formed by the 1898 consolidation of its boroughs. Between 1892 and 1954 more than 12 million immigrants entered the United States through [[Ellis Island]].

Anchored by [[Wall Street]] in the Financial District, the city is a global center of finance, commerce, technology, media, culture, and fashion. The metropolitan area had a gross metropolitan product of over US$2.44 trillion in 2024, larger than the economy of all but nine countries. The [[New York Stock Exchange]] and [[Nasdaq]] are the world's two largest stock exchanges by market capitalization of listed companies. The city is the headquarters of the [[United Nations]]. It also faces concerns about affordability and leads the world in urban automobile traffic congestion despite its 24/7 rapid transit system.

Three physical laws describing the relationship between the motion of a body and the forces acting on it, forming the basis of Newtonian mechanics. They were first stated by [[Isaac Newton]] in *[[Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica]]* (Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy), published in 1687, and Newton used them to investigate and explain the motion of many physical objects and systems.

The first law, often called the law of [[Inertia|inertia]], states that a body remains at rest, or in motion at constant speed in a straight line, unless acted upon by a force. It builds on earlier ideas of Galileo. The second law states that at any instant the net force on a body equals its mass multiplied by its acceleration, F = ma, or, equivalently, the rate at which its [[Momentum|momentum]] changes with time. The third law states that when two bodies exert forces on each other, the forces have the same magnitude and opposite directions. For every action there is thus an equal and opposite reaction, so no force exists in isolation. The third law underlies phenomena from rocket propulsion to collisions.

The laws are usually stated for point or particle masses, bodies whose volume is negligible. This is a reasonable approximation when the separation between bodies is much larger than their size: the Earth and the Sun can be treated as pointlike for the orbit of the former, but not for activities on the Earth's surface. Their mathematical description rests on kinematics and calculus. Velocity is the derivative of position with respect to time, and [[Acceleration|acceleration]] is the derivative of velocity, or the second derivative of position. Position, velocity, acceleration, and force are all vector quantities, having both magnitude and direction. In physics, force is not the same as power or pressure, and mass differs from weight.

The laws enabled precise predictions of planetary orbits, falling objects, and engineering applications. They hold for speeds much less than the speed of light and for scales larger than the atomic. Their limitations led to new theories, namely [[Quantum mechanics|quantum mechanics]] and the [[Theory of relativity|theory of relativity]], which address extreme cases. New insights, especially around energy, built the field of [[Classical mechanics|classical mechanics]] on Newton's foundations.
